author: reek
body: The superblock is written twice, alternating between sector 0 and sector 1 on the parity of its generation number, and boot picks whichever copy is valid and newest. That layout exists for one reason: a machine that loses power partway through a superblock write must still find an intact older copy and come up on it. Nothing tested that the fallback works, and a double-buffered superblock whose second copy is never actually read is one copy with extra steps.

author: reek
body: The old body wrote nothing to disk. It built a FactStore in memory, stored five facts, loaded three back and printed the count -- a chapter named for disk recovery that never touched a sector.

author: reek
body: The corrupt-entry and multi-sector cases in the log itself are already pinned by disk-facts-multi-load; this is the other half, the superblock.

author: reek
body: A superblock is recognised by its magic at offset 0. Overwriting one byte of it is what a torn write looks like from the reader's side: the sector is present and readable, and it is not a superblock.

author: reek
body: Two checkpoints, so both superblock slots hold a real generation and they disagree about how far the log runs. Then the newer slot is torn.

author: reek
body: The fallback answer is deliberately NOT "all four facts". Charlie and delta are on the disk, intact and hash-verifiable, and the recovered store must not report them: the only record that the log extended that far went down with the torn superblock, and a reader that walked past its own log-head would be trusting sectors nothing vouches for. Losing the tail of an uncheckpointed log is the correct outcome. Reading it back anyway would look like a better result and would mean the log-head is not load-bearing.
